title: FHA vs. Conventional Loans: How to Choose the Right One
description: FHA and conventional loans differ on credit, mortgage insurance, and property rules. Here's how to compare them side by side and pick the right one.
image_alt: A modern two-story house with warm lights at dusk

faq.q: Is an FHA loan only for first-time buyers?
faq.a: No. FHA loans are available to any qualified buyer purchasing a primary residence, whether or not it's their first home.

faq.q: Can I remove FHA mortgage insurance?
faq.a: It depends on your down payment. With less than 10% down, FHA annual mortgage insurance generally lasts for the life of the loan; with 10% or more, it lasts 11 years. Many borrowers remove it later by refinancing to a conventional loan once they have enough equity.

faq.q: Which is better for a lower credit score?
faq.a: FHA guidelines are generally more flexible on credit history, while conventional pricing tends to reward higher scores. The better fit depends on your full profile.

body_html:
"Should I go FHA or conventional?" is one of the questions I hear most from first-time buyers. Both can work with a modest down payment. Both are solid, mainstream loans. But they're built for slightly different borrowers, and picking the wrong one can cost you real money over time.

The short version

FHA loans are insured by the Federal Housing Administration and are designed to be forgiving on credit and debt. Conventional loans follow guidelines from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and tend to reward stronger credit with better pricing and more flexible mortgage insurance.

FHAConventional
Credit flexibilityMore forgiving of lower scores and past credit eventsPricing improves noticeably with higher scores
Mortgage insuranceUpfront and annual premium; often lasts the life of the loanMonthly PMI that can be removed as equity grows
Debt-to-incomeOften more room for higher ratiosTypically somewhat tighter
Property typePrimary residence only; condos need FHA approvalPrimary, second homes, and investment properties
Property conditionAppraisal checks health and safety itemsGenerally less strict on minor condition items

Mortgage insurance is usually the deciding factor

With FHA, you pay an upfront premium, usually rolled into the loan, plus an annual premium paid monthly. If you put down less than 10%, that annual premium generally stays for the life of the loan. With 10% or more down, it lasts 11 years. The main way out is refinancing later.

Conventional private mortgage insurance works differently. Its cost depends heavily on your credit score and down payment, and federal law lets you request cancellation once you reach 20% equity based on the original value, with automatic termination at 22%. I break that down further in this guide to PMI and MIP.

That's why the same buyer can see FHA come out ahead with a lower score and conventional come out ahead with a higher one. The only way to know is to price both side by side.

When FHA often makes sense

  • Your credit score is still building or you've had a recent credit event
  • Your debt-to-income ratio is on the higher side
  • You're using gift funds or down payment assistance that pairs well with FHA
  • You plan to refinance once your credit and equity improve

When conventional often makes sense

  • You have strong credit and want mortgage insurance you can eventually drop
  • You're buying a condo that isn't on the FHA-approved list
  • You're buying a second home or investment property
  • The home needs some cosmetic work that could create appraisal conditions under FHA

Don't forget the seller's perspective

In competitive Southern California neighborhoods, some listing agents worry that FHA appraisal requirements could add repair requests. A well-prepared FHA buyer with a strong pre-approval and a responsive loan officer can absolutely compete, but it helps to know the perception exists and address it head-on in your offer.

A side-by-side comparison you can ask for

The fastest way to choose is to ask your loan officer for both options priced on the same day, for the same home, with the same down payment. Then compare these lines:

  1. Total monthly payment, including mortgage insurance, not just principal and interest
  2. Cash to close, including any upfront mortgage insurance and closing costs
  3. How long mortgage insurance lasts on each option, and your realistic path to removing it
  4. What happens if you refinance in a few years, and whether that's likely in your plans

Some buyers find FHA gives the lower payment today while conventional costs less over five or more years. Others find conventional wins from day one. You won't know which group you're in until you see the numbers.

Credit improvement can change the answer

If your credit score is close to a pricing threshold, a small improvement can shift the comparison toward conventional. Paying down card balances before applying is often the quickest lever. My guide on improving your credit before a mortgage walks through what helps and what to avoid. A few weeks of preparation can be worth it if you're not in a rush.

The takeaway

Neither loan is "better" in general. The right choice comes from your credit, your down payment, the property, and how long you plan to keep the loan. Ask for both options priced out on the same day and compare total monthly payment and long-term mortgage insurance cost. That comparison usually makes the decision obvious.
